explanationFacts: Claim c-firms-cut-hiring-not-output: Firms facing improved AI capability respond primarily by reducing hiring and headcount growth rather than by expanding output or redesigning jobs to use the freed-up capacity.

Status is contested because This is an unstated assumption behind the case that AI caused the decline: hiring rates and headcounts cannot by themselves tell 'AI reduced the need for workers' apart from 'AI raised output per worker and firms chose to expand.' The firm-level studies on this map (Hampole et al. on reallocation) do not decide it either. The evidence is not one-sided: U.S. studies of AI adopters find slower junior hiring, the Danish register study does not reproduce it, and the live dispute sits on that gap..

Claim c-targeted-programs-can-help: Better-designed, targeted, employer-linked, long-horizon workforce programs can meaningfully improve displaced workers' earnings and employment, even though generic short retraining programs mostly do not.

Status is contested because The WIA Gold Standard randomized evaluation found that staff-assisted intensive services increased earnings 7%-20%, while evidence on training itself was inconclusive within 30 months. That supports targeted case management, not generic retraining or effectiveness at the scale a national AI-displacement emergency would require..

Claim c-displaced-workers-can-retrain-costlessly: Workers displaced from automated tasks can retrain and relocate into newly created tasks at a cost and delay small relative to the productivity gains.

Status is contested because This is the strongest form of the optimists' assumption that new tasks will absorb displaced workers: adjustment can be costly in absolute terms but small next to the productivity gains, if new tasks and targeted programs work. The retraining evidence on this map finds weak results for ordinary programs, but it does not show that better-funded, employer-linked, AI-specific programs could not do better..
